findings.text: The first paragraph answers what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer can say what Athena is after reading it.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The next step is linked from the header, and the Next steps section is concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, ./setup.sh and a sample `athena ask "add a changelog"`. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: At Athena's own URL, the title and almost all of the page are about a different project, firstmate. Athena itself gets one paragraph, so a newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to judge it mostly by this example of its output.
findings.source: Athena explains how firstmate handles work

findings.text: The lede promises traceable models, a verdict and costs, but the study never shows which models produced it, what the check found or what it cost. Including those would back up the main selling point.
findings.source: It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This link sits in the header, but it is aimed at the site owner, not a visitor. A newcomer may not know whether it applies to them.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The install steps never say to cd into the cloned folder. The page calls Athena 'written in Rust', but the prerequisites list only git, a C linker, curl and Claude Code/npm, with no Rust toolchain, so a newcomer may wonder whether one is needed.

The Start here section, with its 'Words used first' list and its numbered walkthrough of one task, makes the dense firstmate material easy to follow. Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to source lines at a pinned commit, which shows the traceability Athena promises.
The states are listed as bare names and tags such as 'ready waiting', with no definitions. A reader has to go to the Glossary to learn what each state means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work

findings.text: The Limits section says plainly that nothing was run. A careful reader can tell how much weight to give the claims.
findings.source: f1 not run — This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read.

findings.text: The page admits that 'in scope' is undefined, which is honest. But this leaves a gap in explaining when firstmate merges by itself, and the gap shows up in several places.
findings.source: The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it.

findings.text: This refers to a studies/ folder without saying which repository it lives in. A newcomer cannot find it from this page alone.
findings.source: About this page — the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from.
